displayQuote: Thank goodness we don't get as much government as we pay for

meta.title: Who really said "Thank goodness we don't get as much government as we pay for"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Will Rogers died in 1935. The quip first appears in a Nebraska paper in June 1947, quoted anonymously — and wasn't credited to Rogers until 1966.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Thank goodness we don't get as much government as we pay for'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Rogers. Quote Investigator's earliest match is a Nebraska newspaper report of 11 June 1947; Rogers died in 1935 and got the credit only in 1966.

answer.label: Not Will Rogers — an anonymous 1940s tax joke
answer.authorDates: Originator unidentified · earliest match in print, 11 June 1947
answer.sourceLine: There is no Will Rogers source for this line. Rogers died in 1935, and the earliest match located by Quote Investigator ↗ is a report in The Fairbury Daily News of Fairbury, Nebraska on 11 June 1947, where a local businessman named Max Denney passed the quip along to a Rotary meeting as “one man’s observation” — explicitly not claiming it. QI concludes that “an anonymous jokesmith should receive credit for this saying,” and that the 1966 credit to Rogers, arriving so long after his death, is “very weak evidence.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Fairbury Daily News, Fairbury, Nebraska
11 June 1947, page 1, column 8 — “Says Public Interest Answer To Worry Over Tax Burdens”

source.excerpt: The only bright spot in the cost of government Denney said, is one man’s observation that “Thank goodness we don’t get as much government as we pay for”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ ran a dedicated survey of this quip and states: “The earliest match located by QI appeared in a Fairbury, Nebraska newspaper in 1947. Local businessman Max Denney addressed a meeting of Rotarians and discussed government spending. He employed the joke but disclaimed credit.” QI’s conclusion is that “the originator of the saying remains anonymous.”

The trail then runs through Charles F. Kettering, not Rogers: a Birmingham speech reported in the Alabama Journal on 24 January 1949, in which Kettering presented the line as a dialogue between two anonymous men; direct credit to Kettering in The Minneapolis Star of 8 February 1950 and in the U.S. Chamber of Commerce periodical American Economic Security in March 1950; and a Forbes filler item of 15 September 1962. Details and page numbers are on QI’s page ↗.

Will Rogers enters the record only in 1966, in The Clarion-Ledger of Jackson, Mississippi (19 July 1966, page 8): “Will Rogers, the late great humorist, used to say ‘Thank Heaven we don’t get as much government as we pay for’.” QI notes Rogers died in 1935 and treats the gap as “very weak evidence” (source ↗).

Two independent checks agree. Wikiquote’s Will Rogers page ↗ lists the variant “Be thankful we’re not getting all the government we’re paying for” only in its “As quoted in …” section, sourced to The Wordsworth Dictionary of Quotations (1998) by Connie Robertson — a late compilation, not a Rogers text. And the Will Rogers Memorial Museum’s own “Will’s Quotes” collection ↗, which includes a Politics section, contains no instance of the phrase “pay for” at all.
source.excerptNote: This is the earliest instance located by Quote Investigator ↗, transcribed from The Fairbury Daily News of 11 June 1947 (page 1, column 8) via Newspapers.com. Note the construction: Denney is relaying somebody else’s line, and does not claim it.

source.rightsNote: No public-domain claim is made here, because the sentence has no identified author. The earliest known appearance is a 1947 newspaper report published well after 1931 by an identifiable publisher, and it is quoted above only as a short excerpt documenting the attribution. Will Rogers’s own writings are a separate matter — but this line is not among them.

author.name: Will Rogers
author.kicker: The name it gets pinned on
author.heading: About Will Rogers
author.metaLine: 1879–1935 · American humorist, newspaper columnist and film star
author.bio: Will Rogers was born a citizen of the Cherokee Nation in Indian Territory in 1879 and became, by the 1930s, one of the most widely read commentators in America — a vaudeville rope-twirler turned film star who wrote more than 4,000 syndicated newspaper columns and needled Congress for a living. He died in an airplane crash in Alaska with the aviator Wiley Post in August 1935. That enormous, plain-spoken output on taxes and government is exactly why anonymous political quips keep drifting onto his name — but this one surfaces in print only after his death, and the Will Rogers Memorial Museum’s own quote collection does not carry it.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This quip has been handed to four different famous men, and the two who actually used it in public both said it wasn’t theirs. That is the signature of an anonymous joke acquiring prestige by attachment.

items.why: Rogers died in 1935. Quote Investigator ↗ records no instance during his lifetime; the first credit to him is a 19 July 1966 item in The Clarion-Ledger of Jackson, Mississippi — “Will Rogers, the late great humorist, used to say ‘Thank Heaven we don’t get as much government as we pay for’” — and QI holds that “the long delay meant that this was very weak evidence.”

The General Motors research chief used the joke in a Birmingham, Alabama speech reported in the Alabama Journal on 24 January 1949, but framed it as a dialogue between two anonymous men. Newspapers began crediting him outright the next year — The Minneapolis Star, 8 February 1950 — and Forbes was still printing it under his name in September 1962, per QI’s citation trail ↗.

An 18 April 1963 editorial in the Daily Press of Newport News, Virginia offered it as “Thomas Jefferson’s classic remark: ‘Thank heaven, we don’t get as much government as we pay for!’” Quote Investigator ↗ describes the link to Jefferson as implausible.

items.who: Robert A. Heinlein and the quotation books
items.why: In Expanded Universe (Ace Books; 1980 copyright, cited by QI from the 1982 printing) Heinlein wrote: “Will Rogers told us that we were lucky in that we didn’t get as much government as we pay for. He was (and is) emphatically right.” Random House Webster’s Quotationary then certified the Rogers credit in 2001 by citing the CBS-TV programme Will Rogers U.S.A., 9 March 1972 — a television broadcast, not anything Rogers wrote. Both are documented on QI’s page ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: No Rogers column, telegram, radio script or film line containing this sentence has been produced — not by Quote Investigator ↗, not by Wikiquote ↗, and not by the Will Rogers Memorial Museum’s own quote collection ↗. The earliest instance anyone has found is a 1947 Nebraska newspaper report in which the speaker credits an unnamed someone else.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to Rogers
lead: Rogers spent the Depression writing a daily telegram and a weekly column about what Washington was doing with the public’s money, in a voice everyone recognised. He is therefore a natural magnet for any tidy, folksy line about government waste — the attribution sounds right, which is exactly the condition under which nobody goes looking for a citation.

The paper trail runs the other way. The joke turns up in print in 1947, in a Nebraska Rotary Club report, and the man saying it credits an unnamed someone else. For years afterwards it travels attached to Charles F. Kettering, the General Motors research chief — who also disclaimed it — before being handed to Thomas Jefferson in 1963 and to Rogers in 1966. Robert Heinlein repeated the Rogers version in Expanded Universe, and a Random House quotation dictionary certified it in 2001 by citing a 1972 television programme. Every link in that chain postdates Rogers’s death.
context.detailsSummary: The variant wordings, and the book that put Rogers next to Kettering
detailsBody: Evan Esar’s 20,000 Quips and Quotes (1968) printed a Rogers line about government spending directly above the “as much government as we pay for” quip credited to Kettering. Quote Investigator notes that this adjacency “sometimes leads to confusion between attributions” — while pointing out that the Rogers credit was already circulating by 1966, before the book appeared.

The wording is unusually unstable, which is itself a marker of anonymous origin: “Thank goodness we don’t get as much government as we pay for” (1947), “Better be thankful you don’t get as much government as you pay for” (1949), “we don’t get anywhere near as much government as we pay for” (1953), and the form most often seen today, “Thank heavens we don’t get all the government we pay for.” Quote Investigator opens its article by calling the quip “difficult to trace because its phrasing is highly variable.”
context.pull: Rogers died in 1935. The joke reaches print in 1947 — quoted by a man who said it wasn’t his.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest located match is The Fairbury Daily News (Fairbury, Nebraska), 11 June 1947, page 1 column 8, article "Says Public Interest Answer To Worry Over Tax Burdens", where Max Denney quoted "Thank goodness we don't get as much government as we pay for" as "one man's observation" and disclaimed credit; QI concludes the originator remains anonymous.

Quote Investigator states Will Rogers died in 1935, received posthumous credit in 1966 in The Clarion-Ledger (Jackson, Mississippi, 19 July 1966, page 8 column 1) — "Will Rogers, the late great humorist, used to say 'Thank Heaven we don't get as much government as we pay for'" — and that the long delay makes this very weak evidence.

Quote Investigator documents Charles F. Kettering using the joke in the Alabama Journal of 24 January 1949 as an anonymous dialogue (disclaiming credit), direct credit to Kettering in The Minneapolis Star of 8 February 1950 and American Economic Security of March 1950, and a Forbes filler item of 15 September 1962.

Quote Investigator documents the 18 April 1963 Daily Press (Newport News, Virginia) editorial "It Could be Worse" implausibly attributing the line to Thomas Jefferson, and Robert Heinlein's Expanded Universe (1982 printing, 1980 copyright, page 553) crediting Will Rogers: "Will Rogers told us that we were lucky in that we didn't get as much government as we pay for. He was (and is) emphatically right."

Quote Investigator documents Random House Webster's Quotationary (2001, page 330) ascribing the saying to Will Rogers while citing the CBS-TV programme Will Rogers U.S.A., 9 March 1972; and Evan Esar's 20,000 Quips and Quotes (1968, page 354) printing a Rogers remark adjacent to the quip credited to Kettering.

Wikiquote's Will Rogers page lists "Be thankful we're not getting all the government we're paying for." under its "As quoted in ..." section, sourced to The Wordsworth Dictionary of Quotations (1998) by Connie Robertson; the phrase does not appear in the page's Misattributed section.

The Will Rogers Memorial Museum's "Will's Quotes" page presents a topic-organised collection of Rogers quotations (including Politics) and contains no instance of the phrase "pay for" anywhere in the page source.

Will Rogers was born 4 November 1879 near Oologah, Indian Territory, a citizen of the Cherokee Nation, wrote more than 4,000 syndicated newspaper columns, and died 15 August 1935 in an airplane crash in Alaska with aviator Wiley Post.
Charles F. Kettering was an American inventor and engineer, holder of 186 patents, a founder of Delco, and head of research at General Motors from 1920 to 1947.
